bp: A live commerce stream is half television pitch and half crowded shop counter. The streamer is showing products, keeping the mood moving, and watching a chat where viewers ask practical questions: size, color, shipping, use cases, safety, price, or whether the item just shown is the one being discussed. Click-to-Ask serves that moment. The paper is not only trying to make a chatbot for shopping; it is trying to remove two kinds of delay from the selling process. Before the broadcast, product facts may be scattered across images, descriptions, specifications, and seller notes, so preparing a clean script takes time. During the broadcast, useful viewer questions arrive mixed into a fast stream of comments, and an unanswered question can mean a missed sale. The system therefore treats product promotion as a two-stage information problem: prepare reliable product knowledge before the show, then turn live audience questions into timely answers while the stream is happening.
wh: The hard part is that the needed answer is split across time and format. Some information is available before the broadcast, such as product images, text descriptions, and formal product details. Some information exists only during the broadcast, such as which question a viewer asks, what product is currently being promoted, and what has already been said in this particular stream. A simple question-answering system that only sees the latest chat message may miss the product context. A product database alone is also not enough, because viewers do not ask in database language; they ask short, incomplete, conversational questions. The assistant must also help with promotional copy while staying compliant with platform or business rules, which means it cannot merely generate enthusiastic text. The timing pressure matters too. A streamer cannot pause for a long search or rewrite while viewers wait, so the system must shift expensive organization work offline and keep the live step fast.
naive: A smart beginner might paste all product descriptions into a language model before the stream, ask it to write a promotional script, and then ask the same model live questions as they appear. That would work for clean, slow cases, but it breaks in the real setting described by the paper. Product evidence is mixed across visual and textual sources, so raw descriptions may miss facts shown in images or buried in structured attributes. Live chat is noisy, and many comments are not answerable product questions. Even when a question is real, the model needs to know which product and which recent event it refers to. Without structured preparation and stream memory, the answer can be slow, generic, noncompliant, or detached from what the audience just saw.
ap: Click-to-Ask's central move is to separate the work that can be done before the stream from the work that must be done while the audience is present. Offline, the system reads diverse product material, including more than one kind of signal such as image-based and text-based evidence, and turns it into structured product data. That structure is the anchor: it gives the live system organized facts instead of a loose pile of files. The offline side also generates promotional copywriting that is meant to be compliant, so the streamer begins with prepared language rather than improvising every selling point. Online, the streamer can click a viewer question. That click acts like a selection signal: this is the question worth answering now. The system combines the clicked question, the prepared product facts, and an event-level memory of the stream to produce a real-time answer. The design is practical because it treats live selling as a memory-and-retrieval task under time pressure.
mech: The mechanism begins with product inputs gathered before the broadcast. The abstract says these inputs are diverse and multimodal, meaning they can include different evidence forms rather than just one text field. The offline module processes those inputs and converts them into structured product data: instead of leaving facts scattered, it organizes them into a form the system can search and reuse. From that same prepared knowledge, it generates promotional copy that satisfies compliance requirements. This produces two offline outputs: a cleaned product knowledge base and ready-to-use selling language. During the stream, viewer messages appear continuously. The streamer does not ask the system to answer every message automatically; the interface lets the streamer click on a question. That click narrows the problem from a noisy chat stream to one selected audience need. The online module then reads the clicked question against the structured product data and against an event-level historical memory maintained in a streaming architecture, which means the system keeps a running record of relevant events from the broadcast instead of treating each question as isolated. It uses those sources to form a response that fits the product and the current stream context. The output is an answer the streamer can use quickly, while the broader system also supports preparation through generated promotional copy.
math: The mathematical ideas are information organization, matching, sequence memory, and constrained generation. Information organization appears because raw product material must be changed into a structured form. The ordinary operation is sorting facts into fields and relationships so later questions can find the right fact quickly. Matching appears when a clicked question must be paired with the relevant product facts. This is not just word overlap; the useful match is the fact that answers the viewer's intent, such as availability or product property, even if the viewer phrases it casually. Sequence memory appears because a live stream unfolds over time. A question may depend on what was just shown or said, so the system needs a compact record of recent events. The tradeoff is memory versus clutter: keep too little and the answer loses context; keep too much and irrelevant moments can confuse the answer. Constrained generation appears in promotional copywriting and question answering. The system must produce fluent text, but the text is only useful if it stays tied to product evidence and compliance rules. The paper's reported question recognition accuracy and response quality score are measurements of two linked steps: first, identifying the question correctly, and second, producing an answer judged useful.
dots: This paper sits where several conference threads meet. In the Advertising & E-commerce family, it shares the pressure of turning product information into action at the moment a buyer is deciding. Papers such as Campaign-2-PT-RAG and e-commerce relevance work also face the problem that commercial language does not map cleanly onto product records; Click-to-Ask brings that pressure into a live broadcast. In the Multimodal & Vision-Language family, it matches the broader move of using both visual and textual product evidence rather than trusting a single description field. In the LLM Agents & Tool Use family, it resembles production shopping agents: a user asks, the system retrieves or uses prepared knowledge, and a response must arrive under latency and reliability constraints. It also connects to information and matching concepts in the repo: the system decides which chat question deserves attention, which product facts answer it, and which recent stream events should remain in memory.
ww: The design should improve over the naive approach because it puts each kind of work at the time when that work is cheapest and least risky. Product understanding is relatively stable, so doing it offline lets the system spend more effort collecting, cleaning, and structuring facts before viewers are waiting. Live interaction is unstable and time-sensitive, so the online module keeps the live task narrow: respond to the clicked question using prepared facts and recent stream memory. This reduces the chance that the system will search through messy raw material in the middle of a broadcast. The streamer's click also adds human control. Instead of automatically reacting to every chat message, the assistant answers the question the streamer chooses, which helps avoid wasting responses on irrelevant comments. The event-level memory gives the answer situational grounding: if the streamer has just discussed a feature, the answer can reflect that context. The reported TikTok-frame results support this split, with high question recognition accuracy and a strong response quality score on the authors' collected dataset.
po: The payoff is a more usable live-selling workflow. Before the show, streamers spend less time turning scattered product material into promotional language. During the show, they can answer viewer questions promptly by clicking on them, instead of manually searching product details or improvising. The paper grounds this claim in a collected dataset of TikTok live stream frames, where Click-to-Ask reaches 0.913 question recognition accuracy and a 0.876 response quality score. Those numbers do not prove every deployment will raise sales, but they show that the system can recognize questions and produce useful responses well enough to be plausible as a practical assistant for live commerce.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The offline product information has to be accurate and complete enough that structured data can support trustworthy answers. Compliance rules must be represented well; otherwise generated promotional copy may still make unsafe or disallowed claims. The live memory must capture the right events without keeping irrelevant chatter that could mislead answers. The streamer-click interface assumes a human can notice and select important questions in time. The abstract reports results on the authors' collected TikTok live stream frames, so performance on other platforms, languages, product categories, seller styles, and higher-volume chats is not proven here. The abstract also reports recognition and response quality, not long-term business outcomes such as conversion, refunds, buyer trust, or moderation failures.
